'''Iron Finance''' was a [[decentralized finance]] (DeFi) protocol on the [[Polygon (blockchain)|Polygon]] blockchain.<ref name="auto1">{{cite report |last1=Saengchote |first1=Kanis |date=16 July 2021 |title=A DeFi Bank Run: Iron Finance, IRON Stablecoin, and the Fall of TITAN |ssrn=3888089 }}</ref>

==History==
Iron Finance was founded by anonymous developers as a fork of the Frax protocol.<ref name="auto3">{{Cite web|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2021-06-17/mark-cuban-defi-iron-finance-crashed-100|title=Mark Cuban DeFi: Iron Finance Crashed 100% |date=June 18, 2021|website=Bloomberg|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210618161148/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2021-06-17/mark-cuban-defi-iron-finance-crashed-100 |archive-date=18 June 2021 }}</ref><ref name="auto">{{cite journal |last1=Saengchote |first1=Kanis |last2=Samphantharak |first2=Krislert |date=June 2024 |title=Digital money creation and algorithmic stablecoin run |journal=Finance Research Letters |volume=64 |pages= |doi=10.1016/j.frl.2024.105435 |article-number=105435}}</ref> Its early investors included [[Mark Cuban]].<ref name="auto3"/> 

In June 2021, the value of the protocol's tokens collapsed after large holders began liquidating their TITAN positions at peak prices, causing both the IRON [[stablecoin]] and TITAN token to fall sharply.<ref name="auto2">{{Cite web|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2021/06/24/why-titan-crypto-crash-that-burned-mark-cuban-may-not-signal-similar-bitcoin-plunge.html|title=Why the crash of crypto token 'titan' that burned Mark Cuban may not foretell a bitcoin plunge|first=MacKenzie|last=Sigalos|date=June 24, 2021|website=CNBC}}</ref><ref name="auto"/> The situation worsened when a [[smart contract]] malfunction temporarily prevented holders from redeeming IRON.<ref name="auto2"/>

Iron Finance denied that the collapse was a [[rug pull]], stating in a blog post that it resulted from a [[bank run]] triggered by the protocol's algorithmic design.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Locke|first1=Taylor |date=18 June 2021 |title=‘People have been participating without understanding the risks’: Here’s what to know about cryptocurrency-based DeFi |website=CNBC |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2021/06/18/whats-defi-crypto-based-decentralized-finance-explained.html|access-date=14 October 2025}}</ref> ''[[Forbes]]'' described the event as a "wave of panic selling" after major investors sold large volumes of TITAN. The price decline exposed a design flaw that created [[arbitrage]] opportunities, accelerating further sell-offs.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Ponciano|first1=Jonathan |date=17 June 2021 |title=Mark Cuban ‘Hit’ After Cryptocurrency Crashed 100% In One Day—And These Other Buzzy Tokens Have Also Collapsed |website=[[Forbes]] |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/jonathanponciano/2021/06/17/mark-cuban-backed-cryptocurrency-crashed-100-in-one-day-and-these-other-buzzy-tokens-have-also-collapsed/|access-date=14 October 2025}}</ref>

== Tokens ==
IRON was an [[algorithmic stablecoin]] backed by 75 percent USDC and 25 percent TITAN. The Target Collateral Ratio (TCR) determined the proportion of USDC required to mint $1 worth of IRON, with the remainder supplied by TITAN at market value.<ref name="auto1"/> Users could redeem IRON for USDC and TITAN based on the Effective Collateral Ratio (ECR), which reflected the proportion of USDC per $1 of IRON redeemed. Both ratios adjusted based on IRON's price relative to its $1 peg and the protocol's USDC reserves.<ref name="auto1"/>

TITAN was the protocol's native token and had no governance or ownership rights. It was required for minting IRON and could be staked in liquidity pools to facilitate trading.<ref name="auto1"/>

The protocol's partial-collateral model contributed to its failure.<ref name="Di Maggio">{{Cite book |title=Blockchain, Crypto and DeFi: Bridging Finance and Technology |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Uq8kEQAAQBAJ&dq=%22iron+finance%22&pg=PA198 |last=Di Maggio |first=Marco |year=2024 |isbn=9781394275908 |pages=198–199| publisher=John Wiley & Sons }}</ref> A rapid increase in TITAN's price prompted large holders to sell, which triggered a [[negative feedback loop]] known as a "death spiral."<ref name="Di Maggio"/> TITAN's value fell to near zero, and IRON lost its dollar peg. The collapse resulted in an estimated $2 billion in losses and is widely cited as the first major DeFi "bank run."<ref name="Di Maggio"/><ref name="Ross2022"/>

== Liquidity pools ==
Iron Finance operated four liquidity pools across three pairs: USDC–IRON (two pools), TITAN–IRON, and TITAN–MATIC.<ref name="auto1"/><ref name="Ross2022">{{Cite book |title=A Beginner's Guide to High-Risk, High-Reward Investing |last=Ross |first=Robert |publisher=Simon and Schuster |year=2022 |isbn=9781507218235 |pages=241–243 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uC9qEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22iron+finance%22&pg=PA242}}</ref> Liquidity providers earned TITAN as incentives.<ref name="auto1"/>

== Tokenomics ==
Iron Finance planned a total supply of 1 billion TITAN tokens. Of these, 700 million were allocated as rewards over 36 months, and 300 million were reserved for protocol sponsors, vesting linearly over 12 months.<ref name="auto1"/>
